analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $12 and later to the national median, and ends the separate tipped wage.
analysis.headline: The Raise the Wage Act, which would have stepped the federal minimum wage up to $12 an hour and eventually to the national median wage, was referred to a House committee in 2015 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in steps from $7.25 an hour to $8.00, then $9.00, $10.00, $11.00, and $12.00 over four years. After five years, the wage would rise automatically each year along with the median hourly wage of all American workers, so it would keep up with typical pay. It would also phase out the lower 'tipped' minimum wage, eventually requiring restaurants to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage and guaranteeing workers the right to keep their tips. The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, including many in restaurants, retail, and care work. Tipped workers such as servers would gain the most, because the separate $2.13 tipped wage would eventually disappear and their employers would owe them the full minimum wage directly.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $8.00 in the first year, then $9.00, $10.00, $11.00, and $12.00 over four years [S2][S3].

After five years, ties the minimum wage to the median hourly wage of all employees as measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, so it rises automatically with typical pay instead of waiting for Congress to act [S2][S3].
Raises the tipped minimum wage to $3.15 and then by annual steps until it equals the full minimum wage, ending the separate tipped wage entirely [S2][S3].
Guarantees employees the right to keep their tips and requires employers to tell workers about that right [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay at or near the federal minimum, especially restaurants that currently pay the $2.13 tipped wage and count tips toward their payroll obligation, would face higher direct wage costs. Supporters argue higher pay reduces turnover and boosts customer spending, which offsets part of the cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise employers' direct wage costs, and restaurants using the tipped system would see the largest shift, since they would owe the full minimum wage in cash rather than relying on tips to cover it [S2][S3].

Some economists warn that a large mandated wage increase can lead employers to cut hours, automate, or raise prices, effects the bill does not address; the bill includes no small-business transition aid beyond the phased-in schedule [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: workers at the bottom of the pay scale earn more, including tipped workers who today can legally be left with as little as $2.13 an hour in cash wages. The main cost falls on the employers of those workers, concentrated in restaurants and other low-margin businesses, and the phased four-year schedule plus an automatic link to median wages spreads the increase out. The strongest objection is uncertainty about job effects in the lowest-wage sectors, but the bill's structure — gradual steps and a formula tied to overall wage growth rather than a fixed high number — is a moderate version of the idea rather than an abrupt shock.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no vote ever happened in the committee or on the House floor before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 30, 2015 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S5].
On November 16, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote afterward [S5].
175 House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats [S4].
Congress ended on January 3, 2017 without the bill ever receiving a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the federal minimum or the $2.13 tipped wage, especially restaurants, kept the existing wage floor for the full two-year Congress because the bill never advanced to a vote. Workers paid at those rates kept earning $7.25 or less per hour in base wages.

for.name: Bobby Scott
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it with 174 original cosponsors on April 30, 2015.

for.name: 175 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including the top House Democratic leadership (Pelosi, Hoyer, Clyburn)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over wage legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a committee vote; it was sent to a subcommittee in November 2015 and stayed there.

sides.party_line_note: All 175 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority and the committee gavel, the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would phase out the $2.13 tipped minimum wage, requiring restaurants to pay servers the full federal minimum in cash. Restaurants that rely on tips to cover payroll opposed this type of change, while servers would see a guaranteed base wage.
The bill would raise the wage floor these employers owe workers by 66% over four years, increasing direct labor costs. Workers in these sectors are the main beneficiaries.
